tip: Τι κάνεις (ti kaneis) is literally 'what are you doing?' – it's the everyday 'how are you?'. The standard reply: καλά (kala = fine).
Γεια σου (geia sou) is for one friend – with a group or a stranger it becomes γεια σας (geia sas).
Καλησπέρα (kalispera) takes over from late afternoon on – καλημέρα (kalimera) covers morning to early afternoon.
Καληνύχτα (kalinychta) is only for parting at night – to greet someone in the evening, use καλησπέρα (kalispera).
The -ετε (-ete) ending is the polite form: τι κάνετε (ti kanete) with strangers and elders, τι κάνεις (ti kaneis) with friends.
Χαίρετε (chairete) is a polite all-purpose hello – safe with strangers, officials, anyone whose formality level you can't guess.
Με λένε (me lene) is literally 'they call me' – the everyday way to say 'my name is' in Greek.
Σας λένε (sas lene) is the polite way to ask a name; with a friend it drops to σε λένε (se lene).
Ονομάζομαι (onomazomai) is the slightly formal 'my name is' – everyday speech prefers με λένε (me lene).
Greek puts 'the' before names: η Σοφία (i Sofia), literally 'the Sofia'. Skipping the article sounds off.
Nationality words change with gender: a Greek woman is Ελληνίδα (Ellinida), a Greek man is Έλληνας (Ellinas).
No 'you' needed – the -ς (-s) ending of μιλάς (milas) already says it. Greek drops words like 'I' and 'you' unless emphasizing.
No 'a' before jobs in Greek: είμαι δάσκαλος (eimai daskalos) is literally 'I am teacher'. Same with any profession.
Many job words have a feminine form: δασκάλα (daskala) for a woman, δάσκαλος (daskalos) for a man.
Adjectives match the speaker: a man says κουρασμένος (kourasmenos), a woman κουρασμένη (kourasmeni).
With neuter nouns the adjective ends in -ο (-o): το παιδί είναι άρρωστο (to paidi einai arrosto).
Plural adjectives mark the group's gender: χαρούμενοι (charoumenoi) for men or a mixed group, χαρούμενες (charoumenes) for women only.
Δεν (den) right before the verb makes it negative: δεν είμαι (den eimai) = I am not. That's the whole system – no 'do' needed.
Εγώ (ego) is pure emphasis – είμαι (eimai) alone already means 'I am'. Adding it sounds like 'I, for one'.
Θα (tha) turns the present into the future: θα είμαι (tha eimai) = I will be. No ending changes – just add θα (tha).
Greek uses the plain present for near plans: μιλάμε αύριο (milame avrio) is literally 'we talk tomorrow' – no 'will' needed.
Παρακαλώ (parakalo) means both 'please' and 'you're welcome' – it's the standard reply to ευχαριστώ (efcharisto).
Συγγνώμη (syngnomi) does double duty: 'sorry' for mistakes and 'excuse me' to get someone's attention.
Γεια σας (geia sas) works both coming and going – it's 'hello' and 'goodbye' alike, like Italian ciao.
Τα λέμε (ta leme) is literally 'we say them' – 'them' meaning the things you'll talk about. It's the everyday 'see you / talk soon'.
'A/one' changes with gender: έναν αδερφό (enan aderfo = a brother), μία αδερφή (mia aderfi = a sister), ένα παιδί (ena paidi = a child).
Μου (mou = my) comes after the noun: η οικογένειά μου (i oikogeneia mou), literally 'the family my'.
Εσείς (eseis) and the -ετε (-ete) of έχετε (echete) are the polite-or-plural 'you': one person you respect, or several people.
Αυτή (afti) is 'this one' for feminine words – it matches γυναίκα (gynaika = woman/wife). A neuter word would take αυτό (afto).
Του (tou = his) follows the noun: η γυναίκα του (i gynaika tou), literally 'the wife his'.
Στην (stin) is σε (se) + την (tin) squeezed together: στην τσάντα (stin tsanta) = in the bag. Greek always contracts σε (se) with 'the'.
Greek 'the' changes with gender: η (i) goes with feminine words like η βαλίτσα (i valitsa = the suitcase).
Το (to) is the neuter 'the': το βιβλίο (to vivlio = the book). Στο (sto) = σε (se) + το (to), 'at the'.
Ο (o) is the masculine 'the': ο υπολογιστής (o ypologistis = the computer). The adjective matches too: παλιός (palios = old).
Αυτό (afto) is 'this one' for neuter words – it points at το τηλέφωνό μου (to tilefono mou = my phone).
Masculine 'the' switches ο (o) to τον (ton) when the noun is the object: θέλουμε τον λογαριασμό (theloume ton logariasmo).
Place names carry the article: για την Αθήνα (gia tin Athina) is literally 'for the Athens'.
Να (na) links verbs where English uses 'to': θέλω να πάω (thelo na pao = I want to go). Greek chains verbs with να (na), not a 'to' form.
The verb after να (na) carries its own person: θέλεις να πάμε (theleis na pame) = you want US to go – πάμε (pame) already says 'us'.
'This X' keeps 'the': αυτό το βιβλίο (afto to vivlio) is literally 'this the book' – the article never drops.
Article + adjective stands alone: θέλω το μικρό (thelo to mikro) = I want the small one. Greek has no word for 'one' here.
The accent matters: πού (pou) with an accent asks 'where'; unaccented που (pou) means 'that/which'.
'Who' matches gender: ποιος (poios) for masculine like ο γιατρός (o giatros), ποια (poia) feminine, ποιο (poio) neuter.
The accent flips the meaning: πώς (pos) asks 'how', as in πώς πας (pos pas = how do you get there); unaccented πως (pos) means 'that'.
Swap the little word to ask about others: πώς τον λένε (pos ton lene) is literally 'how do they call him' – what's his name.
